opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think the answer has shifted quite a bit over the last few years.

In the more classical pipeline, you'd watch a human do a task, then extract some structured representation from it: object poses, hand trajectories, contact points. A planner or controller would consume that. In that world, precise state estimation is everything. If your 6D pose estimate of a mug is off by a centimeter, the grasp fails. The whole system is only as good as the perception module feeding it, because the learning happens on top of an explicit state.

When you move toward end-to-end visuomotor policies, where you learn directly from pixels to actions, much of that burden shifts. The policy doesn't need to know the exact pose of the object in some global frame. It needs to learn what visual features matter for the action. Closed-loop feedback also does a lot of the work. If the policy is reactive and running at a reasonably high frequency, it can correct small errors as it goes, the way humans do. We don't estimate the precise 3D pose of a cup before picking it up. We reach roughly, look, and adjust.

But it doesn't go away entirely, especially when learning from human data rather than robot teleoperation. With human videos or egocentric data, you have an embodiment gap. To transfer anything useful, you still need some correspondence: where the hand is, how it's oriented, what it's contacting. Hand pose estimation, camera pose, and some notion of 3D structure become the bridge between the human and the robot. So precision matters there, but in a different way. You need it to align the two embodiments in a shared space, not necessarily to drive control directly.

So I'd frame it as a spectrum. The more you rely on explicit, modular representations, the more precise your state estimation has to be. The more you rely on learned, closed-loop policies trained with lots of data, the more you can tolerate noisy or implicit state. And human data sits in an interesting middle ground. It's abundant and diverse, which is why we want it, but using it well still needs enough structure to cross the embodiment gap. Much of the interesting research right now is about how little explicit state you can get away with while still extracting useful signal from how people move and interact with the world.

r001.rationale: The response says human data needs some precise correspondence to bridge the embodiment gap, but does not state that treating human data as robot teleoperation data requires more precise state estimation.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe using human data only to demonstrate a task, or condition reduced precision on the robot already knowing how to reach every constituent state.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's actually a question I think about a lot, because I think the answer has shifted over the past few years.

The classical robotics pipeline is very explicit about state. You estimate where the objects are, what the robot's pose is, maybe the contact state, and then you plan and control on top of that representation. In that paradigm, precise state estimation is the whole game. If your estimate is off by a centimeter, your grasp fails, and the downstream planner has no way to recover because it's reasoning over a world that doesn't match reality.

When you move to learning from human demonstrations, especially end-to-end imitation learning where the policy maps directly from raw observations to actions, something interesting happens. The policy never has to commit to an explicit state. It learns whatever intermediate representation is useful for reproducing the behavior in the data. So in some sense the need for precise state estimation goes down, because the model is doing an implicit, task-specific version of it that only has to be as precise as the task demands. Humans do this too. When you pick up a mug, you don't compute its six-degree-of-freedom pose to millimeter accuracy. You get close, you use contact and vision to correct, and you're done.

But I'd push back on the idea that the need disappears. It just moves. It moves into the data. If humans demonstrate with a teleoperation rig, the quality of your "state estimation" is now about how faithfully the demonstration captures what the human actually intended and perceived. If you learn from human videos, you have a much harder problem, because you have to bridge the gap between a human hand and a robot gripper, and that often requires recovering some structured representation of hand pose, object pose, contact, and so on. So the more indirect the human data is, the more you end up reintroducing explicit state-like quantities, not for control, but to make the data usable at all.

The other place it comes back is generalization and robustness. A pure end-to-end policy is only as precise as its training distribution. When you get out of distribution, there's no principled mechanism for it to say "I'm uncertain about where the object is." Methods that maintain some structured intermediate, whether that's keypoints, object-centric representations, or even a learned latent that behaves like a state, tend to give you better levers for handling those failures, for composing skills, and for long-horizon tasks where errors compound.

So my view is that the amount of explicit state estimation you need is inversely related to how closely your learning signal matches the robot's own embodiment and sensors, and how short-horizon and reactive the task is. Teleoperated data, short tasks, you can get away with very little. Human video, long-horizon manipulation, you're going to want structure, even if it's learned rather than hand-engineered. The interesting research question to me isn't whether we need state estimation, it's what level of abstraction the state should live at, and whether we can let the data decide that rather than deciding it ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response says teleoperated data can require very little explicit state estimation and that more indirect human video data may require structured representations. It does not state that extending the paradigm of treating human data as robot teleoperation data requires more precise state estimation.

r002.rationale: The response says end-to-end imitation can reduce the need for explicit state estimation, but does not state that human data used only to show a task needs less precision when the robot already knows how to reach every constituent state.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on where the human data enters the learning process. If you’re using it to recover a trajectory that a robot should reproduce, then precise state estimation becomes pretty important. You need to know where the objects are, how the person is moving, and how those movements map onto the robot’s body. Errors in that reconstruction can become errors in the behavior you’re teaching.

But if you’re using human data to learn a task’s structure—what needs to happen, in what order, or what success looks like—you may not need that same level of precision. The robot can learn the details of execution through its own experience and feedback.

So I would separate understanding the human demonstration from controlling the robot. Watching someone put a cup on a shelf can teach you the goal without giving you an exact, executable motion. The robot still needs enough information to grasp and place the cup reliably, but that information doesn’t necessarily have to come from precise state estimation of the human demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response says precise estimation is important when reconstructing human movements into a trajectory the robot should reproduce, capturing the teleoperation-like use of human data.

r002.rationale: It says task structure or goals may need less precision, but does not state the required condition that the robot already knows how to reach every constituent state.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you’re trying to learn from the human data. If you want to recover the exact motion and translate that into a robot trajectory, then precise state estimation matters a lot. You need to know where the objects are, how the hand is moving, and how those motions map onto the robot’s body. Errors in that process can directly affect execution.

But if you’re learning something more abstract—what the person is trying to accomplish, which steps matter, or what a successful interaction looks like—you may not need that same level of precision. You can use human data to learn those higher-level patterns, and then use robot experience and feedback to figure out the actual control.

So I wouldn’t say learning from human data eliminates the need for precise state estimation. It changes where you need it. You might tolerate fairly noisy observations when learning the task, but still need very accurate local feedback when the robot makes contact or manipulates something.

r001.rationale: The response says precise state estimation matters when recovering exact human motion and translating it into a robot trajectory, which conveys the need for greater precision when human data serves as robot motion data.

r002.rationale: The response says higher-level task learning may tolerate noisy observations, but it does not state that this depends on the robot already knowing how to reach every constituent state.
